summary: A list of RFCs by number as of June 1, 1971, giving the first author, title, date and NIC number for each document from RFC 1 onward. It is a reference tool for finding early memos. It was replaced by RFC 200.

eli5.summary: A big table of contents for all the notes written so far, so you can look one up by its number.

questions: where is a list of early rfcs
what was the rfc list by number
subtitle: A comprehensive list of RFCs by number with author and date.

tldr.problem: RFC 160 provided a brief title-based list of early RFCs, but researchers and network engineers needed more detailed information, including each RFC's author and publication date.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 170 provides a table of all RFCs from 1 through 170 (and a few proposals that were never numbered), organized by RFC number, with the first author's name, full title, date of publication, and NIC number for each entry.
tldr.outcome: The expanded index became a more useful reference tool for the ARPA Network community, though it was itself soon superseded by RFC 200, which continued the indexing approach.

today: RFC 170 is Historic. It was quickly replaced by RFC 200 as the RFC collection continued to grow, but it remains a detailed snapshot of early ARPA Network documentation.

sections.title: A Detailed RFC Index
sections.content:
RFC 170 is an RFC List by Number, dated June 1, 1971. It extends RFC 160 by adding author names and publication dates to each entry, making it a more useful reference tool. Each row lists an RFC's first author, its full title, the date it was published, its NIC catalog number, and its RFC number.

The list covers RFCs 1 through 170, plus a few early network documents that were never formally assigned RFC numbers, such as early Requests for Comments that predated the official RFC series or documents that did not receive numbers.
sections.eli5: This is like RFC 160 but better, showing who wrote each note, when it was written, and what it was called.

sections.title: Contents and Organization
sections.content:
The RFC 170 list documents the maturation of the ARPA Network working group over two years. The earliest RFCs (1–10) date from April 1969; by 1970, the RFCs had expanded to cover protocol design, implementation details, meeting notes, graphics systems, and administrative issues. By June 1971, the collection included nearly 170 documents spanning fundamental network work such as the HOST-HOST protocol, the IMP-HOST interface, and early application protocols like Telnet and file transfer.

Some entries note "not yet issued," indicating slots where RFCs were planned but never materialized. The list also captures the RFC series' own growing pains, such as the move to include author names and more complete titles as the collection grew.
sections.eli5: You can see who wrote each note, when they wrote it, and what it covered. The list shows how the network was growing and what people were working on.

sections.title: Quick Reference for the Early Era
sections.content: RFC 170 served as a comprehensive snapshot of the ARPA Network documentation effort as of June 1, 1971. It was a standard reference for the early networking community, quickly superseded by RFC 200 and other later indexes as the RFC collection continued to grow. The historical value of RFC 170 is that it captures the state of the field at a pivotal moment in the development of the ARPA Network.
sections.eli5: This was the big reference table people used to find things, until it got replaced by newer, bigger tables as more notes were written.
